Photograph: mattmcbradley/NBC News West Bank Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home Edward Helmore Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.55 EDT Last modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area. Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”. The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus. Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house. A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks. “They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic. Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated. “Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.” Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village. Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers. Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”. They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said. “The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said. “IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added. Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador. Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills. Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”. According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27927.text: Big News Network.com Roundup: China passes healthcare security law, appoints civil affairs minister, ratifies extradition treaty with Hungary BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Friday voted to adopt a new healthcare security law, approve the appointment of a new civil affairs minister, and ratify an extradition treaty with Hungary. The votes were taken at a closing meeting of the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC) in Beijing. Lawmakers also voted to adopt a law on farmland protection and quality improvement, a revised Agriculture Law, a revised National Defense Mobilization Law, and a decision on amending the lawyers law. They also adopted a decision to remove Lu Zhiyuan from the post of minister of civil affairs, and appoint Li Changguan as minister of civil affairs. President Xi Jinping signed five presidential orders to promulgate the laws and the decision, and a sixth one to announce the decision on the personnel change. Zhao Leji, chairman of the NPC Standing Committee, presided over the closing meeting. In the meeting, lawmakers ratified an extradition treaty between China and Hungary. The legislature voted to remove Zhang Youxia as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) of the People's Republic of China and Liu Zhenli as a member of the CMC. Lawmakers also voted on several personnel appointments and removals and other personnel-related bills. They also passed a deputy qualification report. While addressing the closing meeting, Zhao said that legislative work should place greater emphasis on safeguarding and promoting social fairness and justice, further improve the socialist legal system with Chinese characteristics, and provide solid legal guarantees for advancing Chinese modernization on all fronts. He stressed the need to strengthen legislation in key, emerging and foreign-related fields, and called for efforts to improve the quality of legislation and ensure that it keeps pace with changing needs. Zhao also chaired a meeting of the Council of Chairpersons of the NPC Standing Committee before the closing meeting, and presided over a lecture for lawmakers afterward. Photograph: Albert Zawada/EPA Poland Donald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detained Polish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealed Agence France-Presse in Warsaw Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.01 EDT First published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 08.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk , said on Sunday that a man accused of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister had been detained. “The man threatening an attack has been detained,” Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their “swift and decisive action”. The arrest was also confirmed by the country’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński. The interior ministry had earlier said that Tusk and the defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been targeted. It ordered authorities to take action “in connection with the information received by the police concerning a possible assassination attempt on the prime minister... as well as the deputy prime minister”, who is also defence minister, spokesperson Karolina Gałecka wrote on X. Members of the police, state protection service (SOP) and internal security agency were present at Sunday’s meeting. “We are treating this matter as deadly serious,” a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzyński, told journalists afterwards. “Month by month, year by year, more and more various threats and menacing messages reach the police, SOP, and the services concerning Poland and Poles,” he said. In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out.” Poland, a Nato and EU member, has been on high alert after a series of stabbings in the last week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a “cult of violence”. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c95y.text: Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishes By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 24 October 2026 Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said. After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux. But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history. The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000. Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them Published 3 days ago Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched. President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism. Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership. French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported. Image source, EPA Image caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in Bordeaux In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city. Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux. In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture. "There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city. NuÃ±ez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase. The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office. "They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said. Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government. "I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police." He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France". Image source, Reuters Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans which proceeded peacefully. Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday. In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels. In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops. Image source, EPA Image caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux. Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests. Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured. The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities. The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers. The final person to undergo treatment for the disease in Kenya had 11 contact cases, Duale said, who will also undergo 21 days of quarantine. Kenya will be declared Ebola-free on December 23 if no one else exhibits symptoms until then. "Through strengthened surveillance and contact tracing, all 135 contacts linked to the index case were successfully traced and monitored," the health ministry said. "All nine confirmed cases remained within a single transmission cluster, with no community transmission recorded," it added. Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The first of its nine cases, reported on October 6, came from a Kenyan man who had recently travelled back from the Demoratic Republic of Congo . Seven patients recovered, and two passed away. What is the state of the Ebola outbreak? DR Congo on Wednesday reported 11,000 cases of the virulent, often fatal disease. This current outbreak , which began in May, has become Congo's deadliest, claiming 5,387 lives so far. There has also been one case reported in Nigeria , from a patient who had recently travelled from Uganda, which saw a small cluster of the disease .
